With that range of group sizes I'd be a little leery of the regression=20
approach even though it is using ln(group size). If it was me I'd focus =

on using ln(group size) as a covariate in mcds. Doing some simulation=20
may be helpful. I've never dealt with anything with that kind of=20
range.--jeff

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: Generating an estimate of expected cluster size given
parts:
Brendan, the usual problem with large aggregations of seaduck (aside from e=
stimating the number of birds in a cluster) is that you cannot sensibly ide=
ntify a single location for a cluster. Even if you can, then the effective=
width of search for the really large aggregations is an order of magnitude=
larger than for small groups. You can in principle stratify by cluster si=
ze - e.g. 3 strata, of small, medium and large clusters, possibly with the =
3rd stratum being treated as a strip transect (complete count within the su=
rveyed strip). But number of detected clusters is then typically very smal=
l, perhaps just one, for the large cluster stratum. Also, such large clust=
ers can extend across more than one transect line.

Using aerial visual surveys, the best strategy is perhaps to collect distan=
ce data in intervals, e.g. placing markers on the wing struts, with aligned=
markers on the windows, to ensure the observers count birds in the right i=
nterval. You then just count numbers of birds detected in each distance in=
terval, without attempting to record clusters at all.

In the UK, we have switched to using high resolution video or stills, which=
allows a complete count of birds to be done within the strip (which tends =
to be narrower than for visual surveys). The data are then analysed using =
strip transect methods. Again, this avoids the need to define clusters. W=
e also fit spatial density surfaces, e.g. to assess impact of windfarm deve=
lopments.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 136e5b3cd2b9371f
messages.subject: Re: Generating an estimate of expected cluster size given
parts:
Dear Steve Buckland, Brendan and list,

This discussion is very interesting to me, as we were considering using =
distance sampling for 'territories' (aggregation of observations over =
several visits, such as with territory mapping) from point counts. As =
some territories may be large, I think this boils down to a similar =
problem as with large clusters. 'Intuitively', I agree that this is a =
problem for estimating a detection function, and we have decided against =
it.=20
But could you explain exactly what the problem is?=20
Does this have to do with the detection probability not being constant =
(nor necessarily linear) within the large cluster/territory?
And how do you feel about using distance sampling for territories?
If not suitable for species with large territories, is it still =
possible/sensible for species with small territories?
Thank you for any views regarding this topic.

Best regards,


Maja Roodbergen
(Researcher at SOVON Dutch Centre for Field Ornithology)

Brendan, the usual problem with large aggregations of seaduck (aside =
from estimating the number of birds in a cluster) is that you cannot =
sensibly identify a single location for a cluster. Even if you can, =
then the effective width of search for the really large aggregations is =
an order of magnitude larger than for small groups. You can in =
principle stratify by cluster size - e.g. 3 strata, of small, medium and =
large clusters, possibly with the 3rd stratum being treated as a strip =
transect (complete count within the surveyed strip). But number of =
detected clusters is then typically very small, perhaps just one, for =
the large cluster stratum. Also, such large clusters can extend across =
more than one transect line.

Using aerial visual surveys, the best strategy is perhaps to collect =
distance data in intervals, e.g. placing markers on the wing struts, =
with aligned markers on the windows, to ensure the observers count birds =
in the right interval. You then just count numbers of birds detected in =
each distance interval, without attempting to record clusters at all.

In the UK, we have switched to using high resolution video or stills, =
which allows a complete count of birds to be done within the strip =
(which tends to be narrower than for visual surveys). The data are then =
analysed using strip transect methods. Again, this avoids the need to =
define clusters. We also fit spatial density surfaces, e.g. to assess =
impact of windfarm developments.

Steve Buckland

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: Re: Generating an estimate of expected cluster size given
parts:
Maja, that is not really the same issue, as you don't have such a problem o=
f cluster definition. Also, in the seabird case, interest is in how many i=
ndividuals there are, not in how many clusters/flocks there are, whereas in=
your case, you're interested in the number of clusters/territories.

I see no reason why point transect methods would not work for territories. =
You can estimate territory location from e.g. the midpoint of detections t=
hat are deemed to relate to a single territory. If that location is very c=
lose to the point, it seems highly likely that the territory will be identi=
fied even if the bird is not detected at every visit, so certain detection =
at the point seems a reasonable assumption. Variability in detectability d=
epending on where the bird is located inside its territory should not be a =
problem. If territories were very large, then you might need more visits t=
o ensure certain identification of a territory that is centred at the point=
.

In your case, the detection function estimates the probability of detecting=
a territory, as a function of distance of territory centre to the point. =
It is irrelevant how detectability of the bird varies as it moves around th=
e territory, provided the basic assumptions of distance sampling are met: =
a territory is certain to be identified if it is centred at the point; the=
territory location is accurately identified and measured; there is no 'mo=
vement' of the territory in response to the observer. (The latter could oc=
cur if a bird always moved away from the observer on visits, so the cluster=
of detections was systematically shifted further from the point - essentia=
lly in this context, it is the same issue as assumption 2, accurate locatio=
n of territory.)

Steve Buckland
